def: An acute myeloid leukemia subtype (M5) of monoblasts and promonocytes. Characterized by gum hypertrophy, skin infiltration and high serum lysozyme.
Two paired muscles of mastication from the sphenoid bone, supplied by the mandibular nerve. The lateral pterygoid opens and protrudes the jaw; the medial pterygoid closes it.
The smallest skeletal muscle, attached to the stapes and supplied by the facial nerve. It dampens loud sounds; paralysis causes hyperacusis.
A T-cell lymphoma of skin, including mycosis fungoides, with patches and plaques and epidermal Pautrier microabscesses. The leukemic form is Sezary syndrome.
A medullary nucleus that sends climbing fibers to contralateral cerebellar Purkinje cells. Involved in motor learning and coordination.
Complete loss of the sense of taste, as from zinc deficiency, facial nerve injury or viral infection.
The outermost ear ossicle, attached to the tympanic membrane and articulating with the incus. Derived from the first pharyngeal arch.
The lower perilymph-filled chamber of the cochlea, ending at the round window where pressure waves dissipate.
The upper perilymph-filled chamber of the cochlea, beginning at the oval window and separated from the scala media by Reissner membrane.
Cochlear sensory cells that use the motor protein prestin to amplify basilar membrane motion. Damaged by loud noise and aminoglycosides.
Sensorineural hearing loss from prolonged loud noise damaging cochlear hair cells, typically with a notch at about 4000 Hz on audiogram.
The part of cranial nerve VIII carrying balance and head-position information from the semicircular canals and otolith organs to the vestibular nuclei.
Midline brainstem nuclei containing most of the brain's serotonin-producing neurons.
The putamen and globus pallidus together, a wedge-shaped basal ganglia structure lateral to the internal capsule.
A prostaglandin F2-alpha analog eye drop that lowers intraocular pressure by increasing uveoscleral outflow. Causes eyelash growth and iris darkening.
Inability to read with preserved writing, from a left occipital lesion plus damage to the splenium of the corpus callosum, typically after a left posterior cerebral artery stroke.
A localized area of reduced or absent vision within the visual field. A central scotoma occurs in macular degeneration and optic neuritis.
A constitutively active tyrosine kinase produced by t(9;22), the Philadelphia chromosome, in chronic myeloid leukemia. Inhibited by imatinib.
Loss of vision from bilateral occipital cortex damage, with normal pupillary light reflexes and normal fundi. Patients may deny the deficit (Anton syndrome).
Impaired ability to understand or perform arithmetic. Acquired loss (acalculia) from angular gyrus lesions is part of Gerstmann syndrome.
A sudden, severe headache peaking within a minute, the classic presentation of subarachnoid hemorrhage and prompting urgent imaging.
A major protein of CNS myelin and an autoantigen in multiple sclerosis. It may be released into CSF during demyelination.
One of the classical MHC class I genes that present intracellular peptides to CD8 T cells. HLA-A3 is associated with hemochromatosis.
Discrete IgG bands in CSF, absent from serum, showing intrathecal antibody production. Present in most patients with multiple sclerosis.
An injected random polymer of four amino acids that mimics myelin basic protein, used as an immunomodulator in relapsing multiple sclerosis.
A GABA-B receptor agonist muscle relaxant used for spasticity in multiple sclerosis and spinal cord injury. Abrupt intrathecal withdrawal can be dangerous.
A rare fatal brain inflammation years after measles infection, from persistent defective measles virus, causing myoclonus, dementia and seizures.
A component of gamma-secretase on chromosome 14. Mutations cause early-onset familial Alzheimer disease.
A component of gamma-secretase on chromosome 1. Mutations cause early-onset familial Alzheimer disease.
A presynaptic protein whose alpha form aggregates as Lewy bodies in Parkinson disease and Lewy body dementia, and as glial inclusions in multiple system atrophy.
Inability to walk normally despite intact strength and sensation, with feet seeming stuck to the floor. Seen in normal pressure hydrocephalus and frontal lobe disease.
A benign gelatinous cyst at the foramen of Monro in the third ventricle, which can block CSF flow, causing positional headache, hydrocephalus or sudden death.
A normal cell-surface protein (PrPc) whose misfolded, beta-sheet-rich, protease-resistant form (PrPsc) is infectious and causes prion disease.
Fatal neurodegenerative disorders from misfolded prion protein, with spongiform change: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, kuru, Gerstmann-Straussler-Scheinker disease and fatal familial insomnia.
Delivery of focused, high-dose radiation to a small target without incision (for example Gamma Knife), used for brain metastases, arteriovenous malformations and acoustic neuromas.
A neuropeptide from vagal nerve endings that stimulates gastrin release from antral G cells. Also a bombesin-like marker of small cell lung cancer.
The distal stomach before the pylorus, containing G cells that secrete gastrin. Common site of H. pylori antral gastritis.
A duodenal brush border enzyme that converts trypsinogen to trypsin, starting activation of pancreatic zymogens.
The most common malignant salivary gland tumor, usually in the parotid, composed of mucinous and squamous cells; often has a t(11;19) fusion.
Surgical cutting of a muscle, such as Heller myotomy of the lower esophageal sphincter for achalasia.
Surgical splitting of the hypertrophied pyloric muscle to relieve infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (Ramstedt procedure).
Disorders of impaired intestinal nutrient absorption, causing weight loss, steatorrhea and deficiencies. Examples are celiac disease, Whipple disease, tropical sprue and pancreatic insufficiency.
A surgical opening bringing part of the colon through the abdominal wall to divert stool into a bag.
Outpouchings of mucosa through the muscular wall of the colon, usually the sigmoid, at sites where vessels penetrate. Linked to low-fiber diets; can bleed or become inflamed (diverticulitis).
A tumor suppressor on chromosome 5q that degrades beta-catenin. Germline mutation causes familial adenomatous polyposis; an early event in colorectal carcinogenesis.
A tumor suppressor on chromosome 17p that arrests the cell cycle at G1/S after DNA damage or triggers apoptosis. Germline mutation causes Li-Fraumeni syndrome.
A variant of familial adenomatous polyposis with colorectal polyps plus osteomas, soft tissue tumors and congenital retinal pigment lesions, caused by APC mutation.
Endoscopic examination of the esophagus, stomach and first part of the duodenum with a flexible camera.
Ongoing gain or loss of whole chromosomes or large segments, the commonest route to colorectal cancer (APC, KRAS, p53), in contrast to microsatellite instability.
A radiograph of the colon after barium is instilled through the rectum, which can show an apple-core lesion of colon cancer.
Infection with the Chinese liver fluke Clonorchis sinensis from raw freshwater fish, causing cholangitis and raising risk of cholangiocarcinoma. Treated with praziquantel.
An ectodermal thickening in the embryonic head that forms the olfactory epithelium. Failed migration of GnRH neurons from it causes Kallmann syndrome.
A seizure from one brain region with preserved awareness, causing focal motor, sensory or autonomic symptoms.
Epilepsy marked by sudden brief muscle jerks, such as juvenile myoclonic epilepsy on awakening, treated with valproate.
Sustained involuntary muscle contractions causing abnormal posture in one body region, such as writer's cramp, cervical dystonia or blepharospasm. Treated with botulinum toxin.
Involuntary forceful eyelid closure from spasm of orbicularis oculi, a focal dystonia treated with botulinum toxin.
Treatment with a photosensitizing drug activated by light to generate reactive oxygen species, used for actinic keratosis, some cancers and wet macular degeneration.
A pilocytic astrocytoma of the optic nerve, usually in children with neurofibromatosis type 1, causing vision loss and proptosis.
Congenital abnormal collections of vessels without endothelial proliferation, such as arteriovenous malformations and port-wine stains.
A refractive error in which the eye is too short so light focuses behind the retina, blurring near vision. Corrected with convex lenses.
The non-neovascular form of age-related macular degeneration, with drusen and gradual atrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium, causing slow central vision loss.
Age-related macular degeneration with choroidal neovascularization that leaks blood, causing rapid central vision loss. Treated with anti-VEGF injections.
Retinal imaging after intravenous fluorescein dye, showing leaks, blockages and abnormal new vessels.
Brief spinning vertigo on head movement caused by displaced otoliths in the semicircular canals, usually posterior. Diagnosed by the Dix-Hallpike test; treated with the Epley maneuver.
Tumors below the tentorium (cerebellum, brainstem, fourth ventricle), the common location in children: medulloblastoma, pilocytic astrocytoma and ependymoma.
A high-potency dopamine D2 antagonist antipsychotic used for Tourette syndrome. Prolongs the QT interval.
Presence of two or more distinct identity states with recurrent amnesia, usually following severe childhood trauma.
Generalized seizures 6 to 48 hours after stopping heavy drinking, treated with benzodiazepines.
A competitive antagonist at the benzodiazepine site of GABA-A receptors, used to reverse benzodiazepine overdose. Can precipitate seizures in dependent patients.
G-protein-coupled receptors (MT1, MT2) in the suprachiasmatic nucleus that regulate sleep timing. Ramelteon is an agonist.
The most abundant hepatic cytochrome P450 enzyme, metabolizing about half of drugs. Inhibited by grapefruit juice, azole antifungals and macrolides; induced by rifampin.
A volatile anesthetic, now obsolete, that can cause seizure-like EEG activity and fluoride-related kidney toxicity.
An inhaled anesthetic with low blood solubility and a non-pungent odor, giving rapid induction and recovery; popular for children.
An endogenous opioid peptide that acts on kappa receptors, mediating analgesia, dysphoria and stress responses.
Receptors on the presynaptic terminal that modulate transmitter release. Autoreceptors, such as alpha-2 on noradrenergic terminals, generally inhibit further release.
An opioid agonist-antagonist (kappa agonist, mu antagonist) with a ceiling effect on respiratory depression; may precipitate withdrawal in opioid-dependent patients.
An SSRI, the S-enantiomer of citalopram, that blocks serotonin reuptake. Can cause sexual dysfunction, hyponatremia and dose-related QT prolongation.
A tricyclic antidepressant that inhibits norepinephrine and serotonin reuptake. Used for depression, neuropathic pain and migraine prevention; anticholinergic and cardiotoxic in overdose.
A drug acting on serotonin 5-HT1A receptors; buspirone is a partial agonist used for generalized anxiety without sedation or dependence.
An open sore of the cornea from infection (Pseudomonas in contact lens wearers, herpes simplex) causing pain, photophobia and sometimes hypopyon.
The enzyme that degrades GABA to succinic semialdehyde. Inhibited by vigabatrin and valproate.
Small vesicles in the presynaptic terminal that store neurotransmitter and release it by calcium-triggered SNARE-mediated exocytosis. Botulinum toxin cleaves SNARE proteins.
An antiepileptic that inhibits GABA reuptake by blocking the GAT-1 transporter.
A cluster C personality disorder with a pervasive need to be taken care of, submissiveness, clinging and difficulty making decisions.
Dangerous shifts in phosphate, potassium and magnesium, with fluid retention, when feeding resumes in a malnourished patient; insulin surge drives electrolytes into cells.
Sudden loss of muscle tone triggered by strong emotion, such as laughter, with preserved consciousness. Seen in narcolepsy from orexin deficiency.
An atypical antipsychotic (D2 and 5-HT2A antagonist) used for schizophrenia and bipolar depression. Should be taken with food; little weight gain.
Fungal-derived compounds (ergotamine, methylergonovine, bromocriptine) acting on serotonin, dopamine and alpha receptors. Cause vasoconstriction; ergotism can lead to gangrene.
Detecting disease early, before symptoms, to improve outcomes, such as Pap smears and mammography.
A drug that modulates NMDA and GABA signaling to help maintain abstinence in alcohol use disorder. Cleared by the kidneys.
Irreversible acetylcholinesterase inhibition causing cholinergic excess: salivation, tearing, miosis, bradycardia, bronchospasm and fasciculations. Treated with atropine and pralidoxime.
An organophosphate insecticide that irreversibly inhibits acetylcholinesterase, causing cholinergic poisoning.
An uncompetitive NMDA receptor antagonist used for moderate to severe Alzheimer disease to limit glutamate excitotoxicity.
A 5-HT1B/1D agonist that treats acute migraine and cluster headache by vasoconstriction. Contraindicated in coronary artery disease.
Overactive splenic sequestration, often with splenomegaly, causing anemia, leukopenia and thrombocytopenia despite normal bone marrow.
Macrophages lining the liver sinusoids that clear bacteria and debris from portal blood.
Small cationic antimicrobial peptides, made by neutrophils and Paneth cells, that disrupt microbial membranes.
A pelvic autonomic nerve network carrying sympathetic fibers to pelvic organs. Injury can impair ejaculation and bladder function.
A ligament on the side of a hinge joint, such as the medial and lateral collateral ligaments of the knee, resisting valgus and varus stress.
A cytokine from stromal cells that supports development and survival of early B and T lymphocytes.
A classical MHC class I gene. HLA-B27 is associated with seronegative spondyloarthropathies and HLA-B57 with abacavir hypersensitivity.
An MHC class II gene. DR2 is linked to multiple sclerosis and Goodpasture syndrome, DR3 to type 1 diabetes and DR4 to rheumatoid arthritis.
The ability of long-lived memory B and T cells to respond faster and more strongly on re-exposure to an antigen; the basis of vaccination.
The specific part of an antigen recognized by an antibody or T-cell receptor.
Serine proteases delivered by cytotoxic T and NK cells through perforin pores that activate caspases in the target cell, causing apoptosis.
A pore-forming protein released by cytotoxic T and NK cells that creates channels in target cell membranes.
A membrane protein on cytotoxic T cells that binds Fas (CD95) on target cells, triggering caspase-8-mediated apoptosis.
Killing of antibody-coated target cells by NK cells, whose CD16 Fc receptors bind IgG and trigger release of perforin and granzymes.
Mechanisms outside the thymus and marrow that restrain self-reactive lymphocytes, including anergy, regulatory T cells and Fas-mediated deletion.
A protease stored in mast cell granules and released on degranulation; elevated serum levels support anaphylaxis.
Swelling of laryngeal tissues that narrows the airway and causes stridor, seen in anaphylaxis, angioedema and smoke inhalation.
Purified protein derivative of Mycobacterium tuberculosis injected into the skin to test for exposure. The induration reflects delayed type IV hypersensitivity.
An acidic pink dye used in H&E staining that colors cytoplasm and extracellular proteins.
An acute-phase protein whose fragments form AA amyloid in secondary amyloidosis complicating chronic inflammation.
Molecules on all nucleated cells (HLA-A, B, C) that present endogenous peptides to CD8 T cells, assembled with beta-2 microglobulin in the endoplasmic reticulum.
RNA with two paired strands, produced during viral replication and sensed by TLR3; also the genome of reoviruses such as rotavirus.
Antibody-independent complement activation in which spontaneously hydrolyzed C3 binds microbial surfaces, stabilized by properdin to form the C3bBb convertase.
An adhesion molecule stored in endothelial Weibel-Palade bodies and platelet granules that mediates leukocyte rolling.
A blue-green pigment produced by Pseudomonas aeruginosa that generates reactive oxygen species and colors pus.
The skin crease running from the side of the nose to the corner of the mouth, flattened in facial nerve palsy and a site of seborrheic dermatitis.
A mitochondrial inner membrane phospholipid. Anticardiolipin antibodies occur in antiphospholipid syndrome, and it is the antigen in the VDRL syphilis test.
Systemic sclerosis with skin thickening of the distal limbs and face (CREST features), anticentromere antibodies and late pulmonary hypertension.
An overlap of lupus, scleroderma and polymyositis features with Raynaud phenomenon, swollen hands and high anti-U1 RNP antibodies.
An MHC class II allele associated with multiple sclerosis, lupus and Goodpasture syndrome.
Outward bowing of the knees. Physiologic in toddlers; pathologic in rickets and Blount disease.
The joint between the sacrum and ilium, inflamed (sacroiliitis) in ankylosing spondylitis.
The bony prominence of the proximal ulna forming the point of the elbow, where the triceps inserts; the overlying bursa can become inflamed.
Cell-cell junctions of cadherins linked to the actin cytoskeleton through catenins, located just below tight junctions.
A desmosomal cadherin in the superficial epidermis. It is the target of autoantibodies in pemphigus foliaceus and of staphylococcal exfoliative toxin.
A flat brown macule from increased melanocytes along the basal layer, such as solar lentigo; multiple lentigines occur in Peutz-Jeghers syndrome.
A benign vascular tumor of infancy that appears weeks after birth, grows rapidly, then regresses. Stains GLUT1 positive; propranolol shrinks it.
A painful benign tumor of a glomus body (thermoregulatory arteriovenous shunt), typically under a fingernail, with cold sensitivity.
Selective NSAIDs such as celecoxib that block cyclooxygenase-2, causing less gastric injury; contraindicated in sulfa allergy and carry thrombotic risk.
Coronary stents coated with an antiproliferative drug (sirolimus, paclitaxel) to limit restenosis; require prolonged dual antiplatelet therapy.
An intravenous glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitor that blocks platelet aggregation, used in acute coronary syndrome and angioplasty.
An intravenous glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitor that blocks platelet aggregation, used in acute coronary syndrome and angioplasty.
A beta-lactamase that hydrolyzes cephalosporins, such as chromosomal AmpC in Enterobacter and Pseudomonas.
Abnormally wide spacing between the eyes, seen in craniofacial and genetic syndromes such as Noonan and DiGeorge syndromes.
A middle ear muscle attached to the malleus and supplied by the mandibular nerve; it dampens loud sounds.
The largest laryngeal cartilage, forming the Adam's apple; the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve supplies the cricothyroid muscle attached to it.
A statistical test comparing observed with expected counts to assess association between categorical variables.
Antibiotics that inhibit bacterial DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, such as ciprofloxacin and levofloxacin. Risks include tendon rupture, QT prolongation and cartilage damage in children.
A GnRH agonist implant; continuous exposure suppresses LH and FSH. Used for prostate and breast cancer and endometriosis, with an initial flare.
Drugs that block the estrogen receptor, such as tamoxifen, raloxifene and fulvestrant, used in breast cancer and osteoporosis.
A nonhormonal contraceptive whose copper creates a spermicidal inflammatory environment. Can be used for emergency contraception; may cause heavier menses.
Infarction of the optic nerve head causing sudden painless vision loss with disc swelling. The arteritic form is caused by giant cell arteritis.
A cytoplasmic protein that binds tacrolimus; the complex inhibits calcineurin and so T-cell activation. Sirolimus also binds it.
A monoclonal antibody against the IL-2 receptor alpha chain (CD25), used for induction immunosuppression in kidney transplant.
A recombinant G-CSF that stimulates neutrophil production, given after chemotherapy. Causes bone pain.
A monoclonal antibody against CD52 that depletes lymphocytes, used in CLL, multiple sclerosis and transplant; causes infusion reactions and autoimmunity.
Committed marrow precursors (BFU-E, CFU-E) that mature into red blood cells under erythropoietin stimulation.
A pathogen's preference for infecting particular cells or tissues, determined by receptors, such as HIV for CD4 cells with CCR5 or CXCR4.
A far-infrared laser absorbed by water that vaporizes tissue precisely, used in skin resurfacing and surgery.
A tube diverting CSF from a lateral ventricle to the peritoneal cavity to treat hydrocephalus. Complications include infection and obstruction.
Imaging that produces cross-sectional slices of the body, as in CT.
A powerful jaw-closing muscle running from the zygomatic arch to the mandible angle, supplied by the mandibular nerve.
A non-calcium phosphate binder taken with meals to treat hyperphosphatemia in chronic kidney disease.
A hole through the nasal septum, caused by cocaine use, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, surgery or trauma.
Injection of an irritant into varicose veins or esophageal varices to cause fibrosis and closure.
Imaging of the small bowel by swallowing a camera capsule, used in obscure GI bleeding. Risk of retention at strictures.
Drugs such as bortezomib and carfilzomib that block degradation of ubiquitinated proteins, causing apoptosis in multiple myeloma. Cause peripheral neuropathy.
Drugs such as vorinostat and romidepsin that raise histone acetylation, altering gene expression; used in cutaneous T-cell lymphoma.
Study participants who can no longer be contacted or assessed, which introduces attrition bias.
Inspection of the anal canal and rectum with a rigid scope, used to evaluate hemorrhoids and rectal bleeding.
Fluid accumulation in the pleural space, as in hepatic hydrothorax from cirrhosis with ascites.
Liver disease with intrapulmonary vascular dilation and hypoxemia, causing platypnea and orthodeoxia.
Infusion of stool from a healthy donor to restore gut flora, used for recurrent Clostridioides difficile infection.
Chemicals covalently bound to DNA bases, such as from aflatoxin or benzo[a]pyrene, which cause mutations if unrepaired.
Low-energy radiation (radio waves, microwaves, visible light) that cannot remove electrons from atoms; ultraviolet light causes pyrimidine dimers.
The ball-and-socket joint between the humeral head and glenoid, stabilized by the rotator cuff and prone to anterior dislocation.
The shoulder muscle that abducts the arm from 15 to 90 degrees, supplied by the axillary nerve.
Instilling saline into the peritoneal cavity and examining the return fluid for blood, used in trauma evaluation for internal bleeding.
A monoclonal antibody against the RSV fusion protein, given to high-risk infants to prevent severe RSV disease.
An extra rib arising from the seventh cervical vertebra that can compress the brachial plexus or subclavian vessels (thoracic outlet syndrome).
Burning, numbness and tingling of the lateral thigh from compression of the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve, linked to obesity and tight clothing.
Buttock pain and sciatica-like symptoms attributed to the piriformis muscle compressing the sciatic nerve.
The ankle bone between the tibia and fibula above and the calcaneus below. A fracture risks avascular necrosis.
An epithelial chloride channel regulated by ATP and cAMP. The commonest mutation, deltaF508, causes misfolding and degradation, leading to cystic fibrosis.
A proinflammatory cytokine released through the inflammasome that induces interferon-gamma from T and NK cells.
A luminal amebicide used against Entamoeba histolytica cysts and Dientamoeba fragilis.
Infection by Cryptosporidium causing watery diarrhea, severe in AIDS. Oocysts are acid-fast and chlorine resistant; treated with nitazoxanide.
Rickettsia typhi infection spread by rat fleas, causing fever, headache and rash.
A dermatophyte genus (E. floccosum) infecting skin and nails but not hair, causing tinea cruris and tinea pedis.
A dermatophyte infection of the groin with an itchy, red, sharply bordered annular rash that characteristically spares the scrotum.
Candida albicans infection causing itching and thick white curd-like discharge with normal vaginal pH. Pseudohyphae on KOH prep; risk factors include diabetes and antibiotics.
